entries.content:
AI coding agents such as Codex read your codebase, edit multiple files, and run commands and tests while they work through larger tasks with you. In Codex, an AGENTS.md file holds persistent instructions for a project, and config.toml holds the agent's configuration.

We just published a course on the freeCodeCamp.org YouTube channel that will teach you how to get reliable results from a coding agent by giving it the right context, planning the work, controlling its permissions, and verifying every change. This course is taught by Tom Chant, Head of Education at Scrimba.

You'll work through realistic tasks, including challenges on skills, characterization tests, and config.toml. The course is aimed at experienced developers adding AI to their workflow and at non-coders who want to build software with AI help. You can also study it interactively on Scrimba.

In this course, you will learn:

  • Prompting & Project Setup

    How to write effective prompts and comment prompts for a coding agent, then initialize a project and use multiple AGENTS.md files.
  • Plan Mode & Skills

    How to break larger development tasks down with Plan Mode and extend a coding agent with skills.
  • Testing Agent Changes

    How to verify an agent's changes with characterization tests and test-driven development (TDD), and which testing pitfalls to look out for.
  • Git & Secrets

    How to use Git safely alongside a coding agent and keep API keys, credentials, and other secrets safe.
  • Context, Permissions & config.toml

    How to use the VS Code Codex extension, manage context, control what an agent can access and change, and configure it with config.toml.
  • MCP & shadcn

    How to connect agents to external tools with the Model Context Protocol (MCP), including shadcn.

Watch the full course on the freeCodeCamp.org YouTube channel (2-hour watch).

entries.content:
Sending a 5 GB video file might seem simple. You select the file, click Upload, wait for the progress bar to finish, and share a link with someone. But there are several things happening in the background while the file is being uploaded.

The file has to travel across a network, reach a server, and be stored somewhere before another person can download it. The service also needs to make sure that the recipient can access the file without accessing the sender's account. If the internet connection drops halfway through the upload, it needs a way to continue without sending the entire file again.

File transfer services use HTTP requests, storage systems, databases, encryption, and background processes to manage these tasks. But how does a website actually handle a file that's several gigabytes in size? Does it upload everything in one request? Where does the file go after the upload finishes? And what happens when its download link expires?

In this article, we'll look at how file transfer services handle large uploads, store files, generate download links, and manage interrupted connections and expired transfers. Then, once you understand the theory behind how it all works, we'll also build a basic chunked file uploader using Node.js to see some of these processes in action.

What We'll Cover:

Why Email Attachments Fail: SMTP Wasn't Designed for Large Files

Before looking at dedicated file transfer services, it helps to understand why we can't just attach massive files to an email. Sending large files through email is fundamentally flawed because the underlying architecture was built for text, not high-resolution media.

SMTP and Attachment Size Limits

Simple Mail Transfer Protocol (SMTP) handles the transmission of email messages across the internet. Because servers have limited bandwidth and storage, email providers impose strict attachment size limits, usually capping out around 25 MB. However, these limits apply to the encoded message size, not just the original file sitting on your hard drive.

The Base64 Problem

Email attachments are commonly encoded using MIME and Base64 formats. Base64 is necessary because it converts binary data into text-compatible characters that email servers can safely route. While this solves the transmission problem, it creates a massive efficiency issue: this encoding increases the data size by approximately 33%.

You can read the foundational specifications for this in RFC 2045, which defines MIME's Base64 transfer encoding. In practice, this means a 30 MB video file will require roughly 40 MB of space before additional message overhead is even calculated, guaranteeing it will bounce back from most email servers.

The Core Architecture: What Happens Behind a File Transfer Service?

To bypass the limitations of email, file transfer services use a specialized, decoupled architecture. Having built a few of these systems myself, I believe establishing a clear mental model of the five major components is crucial for understanding the flow of data.

The Client

The journey begins in the client, which is usually a web browser or a desktop application where the sender selects a file. Modern browsers use JavaScript's File API to access file metadata, read the raw contents and intelligently divide the file into smaller, manageable parts before any data hits the network.

The Upload Server

Once the client starts sending data, the upload server steps in. This server receives the upload requests, authenticates the user, validates incoming data and coordinates the entire upload process. It acts as the traffic cop, ensuring that chunks of data are arriving in the correct format.

The Storage Layer

Traditional application servers are terrible at holding massive files, so the storage layer handles the actual heavy lifting. Uploaded files are typically routed directly to object storage solutions. This allows the system to scale infinitely without crashing the primary upload servers.

The Metadata Database

While the physical file goes to object storage, the application needs a way to remember what that file is. The metadata database stores critical information, including the original filename, file size, content type, the specific object storage key, a unique transfer identifier and the exact expiration timestamp.

The Download Server

When someone opens a shared link, the download server takes over. It checks the database to verify permissions and expiration dates, and if everything is valid, it retrieves the stored object from the storage layer for delivery.

Chunked and Resumable Uploads: How Large Files Survive Bad Internet Connections

Transferring a 5 GB file in one continuous network request is a disaster waiting to happen. If a connection drops at 99%, a single-request architecture forces the user to start all over again.

Breaking a Large File Into Smaller Chunks

To solve this, modern clients divide large files into smaller parts, such as 10 MB chunks. Each chunk is uploaded to the server as an independent HTTP request. The server meticulously tracks which chunks have arrived. Some advanced systems even allow multiple chunks to upload simultaneously in parallel, drastically reducing the overall waiting time.

It's important to note that chunked uploads are an architectural pattern, which is entirely different from HTTP chunked transfer encoding (a mechanism for framing an HTTP message body).

What Happens When the Internet Disconnects?

Suppose 80% of a massive file has successfully uploaded when your Wi-Fi randomly disconnects. Without resumable uploads, that progress is lost. With resumable architecture, the client reconnects and asks the server for the upload offset, the exact number of bytes successfully received and stored. The client then seamlessly continues uploading from that exact position.

Checksums: Making Sure Nothing Gets Corrupted

Network transfers can sometimes flip bits, resulting in corrupted files. To prevent this, clients generate a cryptographic hash (checksum) for an individual chunk before sending it. The server receives the chunk, calculates its own hash, and compares the two. If the checksums don't match, the server rejects the chunk and asks the client to try again.

If you're looking to implement this, the TUS Resumable Upload Protocol is a fantastic, standardized reference for managing upload offsets and checksum verification. Also, the Amazon S3 Multipart Upload Documentation provides an industry-standard blueprint for handling parallel transfers and retrying failed parts.

Storage and Link Generation: Where Does Your File Actually Go?

Once every chunk is verified and reassembled, the service needs a secure place to keep the file until the recipient is ready to download it.

Why Services Use Object Storage

In my opinion, attempting to store gigabytes of user uploads on a traditional local server directory is architectural malpractice. Instead, services rely on object storage. Files are stored as flat objects and each object is assigned a unique key. Object storage is highly durable and scales quite easily to accommodate millions of massive files simultaneously.

How a Download Link Is Created

The relationship between the stored file and its shareable link relies on the metadata database. When the upload finishes, the application saves the file's storage key in the database and generates a unique access token. The recipient receives a URL containing that specific token. When they click the link, the server reads the token, locates the relevant file in the database and checks the download permissions.

Why Are These Links Difficult to Guess?

A secure file transfer link relies heavily on high entropy, which is randomness that makes tokens mathematically near-impossible to predict. Also, secure systems use signed URLs. These are URLs containing cryptographic signatures that authorize access for a limited, strictly-enforced period.

As outlined in the OWASP Session Management Cheat Sheet, a random link isn't automatically secure without appropriate access controls, expiration policies, and protection against token leakage.

Expiry and Cleanup: What Happens When a Transfer Expires?

File transfer services process petabytes of data, meaning they can't store uploaded files forever without going bankrupt. They rely on aggressive lifecycle management.

Time to Live (TTL)

Every transfer is assigned a Time to Live (TTL) or expiration timestamp. Once that time passes, the database instantly invalidates the transfer identifier, ensuring that the download link no longer authorizes access.

Automated Cleanup Jobs

Because link expiration and physical deletion aren't necessarily simultaneous, background workers or scheduled cron jobs handle the actual cleanup. These workers periodically scan the database to find expired transfers, mark them as permanently unavailable, delete the associated multi-gigabyte objects from the storage layer, and finally remove the outdated metadata.

Download Limits

Some services also allow senders to limit how many times a file can be downloaded. Once the download count reaches the threshold, the link behaves exactly as if the TTL had expired, offering an excellent way to control unauthorized distribution.

Security Layers: Protecting Files During Transfer and Storage

Security in file transfers is never about a single magic feature. It requires multiple layers of defense to keep data safe from interception or theft.

TLS Encryption in Transit

When data travels between the sender, the transfer service, and the recipient, it's heavily encrypted. Modern platforms use HTTPS backed by strict TLS protocols to ensure no one can snoop on the data packets mid-route.

For a deep dive into how this is configured at an enterprise level, NIST SP 800-52 Rev. 2 offers exhaustive guidelines for TLS implementations.

Encryption at Rest

Once the file arrives at the storage layer, encryption at rest ensures that even if a bad actor physically accessed the server hardware, they would only find scrambled, unreadable data. It's important to note that encryption at rest isn't the same as end to end encryption. The service provider still manages the encryption keys in a standard setup.

Password-Protected Links

To prevent unauthorized users from accessing a valid URL, senders can add a password. This creates a secondary access-control layer that must be cleared before the server will even attempt to fetch the file from object storage. Additional safeguards, like rate-limiting against automated password guessing, ensure this layer remains effective.

Real-World Examples: How Popular File Transfer Services Handle File Sharing

Seeing how established companies implement these concepts helps bridge the gap between theory and practice.

WeTransfer: Temporary Transfers and Password Protection

WeTransfer is built entirely around temporary shareable links. Transfers have strict expiration timelines and premium users can enforce password protection. According to their security documentation, they utilize standard TLS encryption during transit and AES-256 encryption at rest to secure files on their servers.

Dropbox Transfer: Sending Files Without Collaboration

Unlike a standard shared folder, Dropbox Transfer creates standalone downloadable links. Recipients don't need a Dropbox account to download the payload. They utilize configurable expiration dates, passwords, and automated download notifications, with maximum file size limits dictated by the sender's specific subscription plan.

Send Anywhere: Direct Transfers and Temporary Links

Send Anywhere takes a fascinating hybrid approach. Its six-digit key transfer mechanism operates in real-time for one-time use within a 10-minute window, often leveraging peer to peer connections. Conversely, its standard Share Link option falls back to a server-based architecture, uploading files and keeping the link valid for up to 48 hours.

Filemail: Large Transfers and Expiration Controls

Offering robust email and shareable-link delivery options, Filemail handles massive payloads easily. They provide highly configurable expiration controls and rigorous password protection. Their free service tier currently allows a 5 GB transfer limit, holding the data securely for a maximum seven-day storage period before automated cleanup takes over.

Hands-On: Build a Minimal Chunked File Uploader Using Node.js

Understanding the theory is great, but building it yourself proves how it actually works. Let's create a simple application that divides a file into smaller chunks in the browser, uploads them to a Node.js server and stitches them back together.

Step 1: Set Up the Node.js Project

You'll need Node.js, the Express framework, and multer for handling incoming file chunks. The built-in fs module will handle our file operations. First, create a Node project and install the required dependencies:

mkdir file-transfer
cd file-transfer
npm init -y
npm install express multer

Step 2: Divide the File Into Smaller Chunks

First, create a 

public
directory inside your project folder if it doesn't already exist. Then, create a file named 
upload.js
inside that directory. We'll use the browser's JavaScript File API and its 
slice()
method to read smaller portions of a file without loading the entire 5 GB payload into your computer's RAM.
const chunkSize = 5 * 1024 * 1024;

async function uploadFile(file) {
    const totalChunks = Math.ceil(file.size / chunkSize);
    const uploadId = crypto.randomUUID();

    for (let index = 0; index < totalChunks; index++) {
        const chunk = file.slice(
            index * chunkSize,
            (index + 1) * chunkSize
        );

        const formData = new FormData();
        formData.append("chunk", chunk);

        const response = await fetch(
            `/upload/${uploadId}/${index}/${totalChunks}`,
            {
                method: "POST",
                body: formData
            }
        );

        if (!response.ok) {
            throw new Error(`Chunk ${index} failed to upload`);
        }
    }

    const response = await fetch(`/complete/${uploadId}`, {
        method: "POST",
        headers: { "Content-Type": "application/json" },
        body: JSON.stringify({
            totalChunks,
            filename: file.name
        })
    });

    if (!response.ok) {
        throw new Error("File reassembly failed");
    }
}

Here, 

crypto.randomUUID()
generates a unique ID for the upload. The browser sends each chunk separately and uses the same ID to associate all the chunks with the original file.

Step 3: Create an Upload Endpoint in Express

On the server side (

server.js
), we need an endpoint to receive and temporarily store each chunk. The server uses the upload ID and chunk index to determine where each part belongs, while the total number of chunks helps validate the upload. We use multer to parse the incoming multipart form data.
const express = require("express");
const multer = require("multer");
const fs = require("fs");
const path = require("path");
const { pipeline } = require("stream/promises");

const app = express();

app.use(express.static(path.join(__dirname, "public")));

const chunksDir = path.join(__dirname, "chunks");
const tempDir = path.join(chunksDir, "temp");

fs.mkdirSync(tempDir, { recursive: true });

const upload = multer({
    dest: tempDir,
    limits: { fileSize: 5 * 1024 * 1024 }
});

app.post(
    "/upload/:id/:index/:total",
    upload.single("chunk"),
    async (req, res) => {
        try {
            const { id, index, total } = req.params;

            if (!req.file) {
                return res.status(400).send("No chunk received");
            }

            if (
                !/^[a-f0-9-]{36}$/i.test(id) ||
                !Number.isInteger(Number(index)) ||
                !Number.isInteger(Number(total)) ||
                Number(total) < 1 ||
                Number(total) > 10000 ||
                Number(index) < 0 ||
                Number(index) >= Number(total)
            ) {
                return res.status(400).send("Invalid upload details");
            }

            const folder = path.join(chunksDir, id);

            await fs.promises.mkdir(folder, {
                recursive: true
            });

            await fs.promises.rename(
                req.file.path,
                path.join(folder, `${index}.part`)
            );

            res.send("Chunk received");

        } catch (error) {
            res.status(500).send("Upload failed");
        }
    }
);

The server stores each chunk using its upload ID and index, making it possible to identify and retrieve the individual parts when the upload is complete.

Step 4: Reassemble the Original File

Once the client confirms all chunks have been transmitted, it triggers a final reassembly route. The server first checks whether every expected chunk exists in the 

chunks/
directory. It then reads the chunks sequentially using 
fs.createReadStream()
and writes them to the same output file using 
fs.createWriteStream()
. The first chunk creates the file, while subsequent chunks are appended to it. Once the original file has been reassembled, the server deletes the temporary chunks to free up space.
const uploadsDir = path.join(__dirname, "uploads");

fs.mkdirSync(uploadsDir, { recursive: true });

app.use(express.json());

app.post("/complete/:id", async (req, res) => {
    try {
        const { id } = req.params;
        const { totalChunks, filename } = req.body;

        if (
            !/^[a-f0-9-]{36}$/i.test(id) ||
            !Number.isInteger(totalChunks) ||
            totalChunks < 1 ||
            totalChunks > 10000 ||
            typeof filename !== "string"
        ) {
            return res.status(400).send("Invalid upload details");
        }

        const folder = path.join(chunksDir, id);

        for (let i = 0; i < totalChunks; i++) {
            const chunkPath = path.join(folder, `${i}.part`);

            if (!fs.existsSync(chunkPath)) {
                return res.status(400).send(`Missing chunk ${i}`);
            }
        }

        const safeName =
            path.basename(filename).replace(/[^\w.-]/g, "_") ||
            "upload.bin";

        const outputPath = path.join(
            uploadsDir,
            `${id}-${safeName}`
        );

        await fs.promises.rm(outputPath, { force: true });

        for (let i = 0; i < totalChunks; i++) {
            const chunkPath = path.join(folder, `${i}.part`);

            await pipeline(
                fs.createReadStream(chunkPath),
                fs.createWriteStream(outputPath, {
                    flags: i === 0 ? "w" : "a"
                })
            );
        }

        await fs.promises.rm(folder, {
            recursive: true,
            force: true
        });

        res.json({
            message: "File assembled successfully"
        });

    } catch (error) {
        res.status(500).send("Reassembly failed");
    }
});

Finally, add the following code at the bottom of 

server.js
to start the Express server:
app.listen(3000, () => {
    console.log("Server running at http://localhost:3000");
});

Step 5: Test the Upload

Start the server by running 

node server.js
in your terminal. Then, open 
http://localhost:3000
 in your browser and select a medium-sized video file to test the upload. Open your browser's Network tab to observe how the file is divided into chunks and sent sequentially. Finally, check your server's 
uploads/
directory. The assembled file should have the same byte size as the original and should open correctly.

Create 

public/index.html
:



    File Uploader


    
Upload a File

Note: This implementation demonstrates the basic mechanics of chunked uploads and file reassembly. It doesn't implement resumable uploads, checksum verification, authentication, object storage, or temporary download links.

A production-grade file transfer service would also require persistent upload states, access controls, retry handling, integrity checks, and automated cleanup.

Conclusion: A Simple Link Hides a Lot of Engineering

Sending a large file involves several processes working together. From upload handling and chunk management in the browser to object storage, metadata tracking, encryption, and automated cleanup, each component has a specific role in making file transfers work.

These processes also explain how services handle interrupted uploads, control access to shared files, and remove data when a transfer expires. Understanding how these components work together makes it easier to see what happens behind the scenes whenever someone uploads a large file and shares a download link.

entries.content:
PDF files are commonly used to share presentations, scripts, reports, lesson materials, comic pages, and other visual documents. But reviewing a long PDF page by page can take time, especially when someone needs to understand the overall sequence of scenes, slides, or visual content.

A storyboard provides a more organized way to review this information. Instead of opening every page individually, users can arrange selected PDF pages into a single sheet containing multiple panels. Each panel can include a page number, a caption, and a visual preview of the original page.

In this tutorial, we'll explore how to build a browser-based PDF Storyboard Generator using JavaScript, PDF.js, and PDF-lib.

The application takes pages from an existing PDF and arranges them into printable storyboard sheets. Users can choose different layouts, select the pages they want to include, add captions, customize the appearance, preview the result, and download the finished storyboard.

The application runs directly in the browser. The uploaded PDF is processed locally rather than uploaded to the website's server.

We'll examine the implementation step by step, including PDF rendering, page selection, caption handling, layout calculations, preview generation, and file export.

What We'll Cover:

What Is a PDF Storyboard Generator?

A PDF Storyboard Generator converts selected pages from an existing PDF into a structured visual sheet.

For example, imagine that you have a PDF containing 20 presentation slides. Instead of sharing all 20 slides separately, you can arrange them into a storyboard containing three columns and two rows per sheet.

Each panel displays a scaled version of its original PDF page. You can also add a number or label and write a short description underneath.

The same approach can be useful for:

  • Reviewing presentation slides.
  • Organizing comic pages.
  • Planning video scenes.
  • Preparing visual scripts.
  • Reviewing scanned documents.
  • Creating printable teaching materials.
  • Organizing page sequences for creative projects.

The application doesn't create new scenes or draw illustrations. It arranges existing PDF pages into a storyboard layout.

Main Features of the Application

Before writing the code, let's understand the features we're going to implement.

1. PDF Upload

Users can select a PDF from their device or drag and drop it into the upload area.

2. Multiple Storyboard Layouts

The application supports three layouts:

  • Grid: Arranges pages in rows and columns.
  • Panels with notes: Provides space for written notes alongside the page panels.
  • Film strip: Arranges pages in a film-strip style.

3. Page Selection and Ordering

Users can choose which PDF pages should appear in the storyboard. They can also specify a custom order rather than following the original PDF sequence.

4. Captions

Users can type captions manually, fill empty captions using extracted PDF page text, or use OCR to read text from scanned pages.

5. Customization

Users can customize the paper size, orientation, number of columns and rows, panel labels, sheet colors, caption font, text size, spacing, and panel frames.

6. Live Preview

The application generates a preview of the storyboard sheets. Users can review the arrangement before downloading the final output.

7. Multiple Export Formats

Users can export their work as:

  • A PDF storyboard.
  • PNG storyboard sheets.
  • A ZIP file containing individual page pictures.

The PDF export preserves original page content as vectors when possible, helping maintain sharp text and graphics.

Understanding the Browser-Based Workflow

The application follows a straightforward process.

  • The user selects or drops a PDF file into the upload area.
  • PDF.js loads the document and renders its pages.
  • The application displays page previews and caption fields.
  • The user selects pages, changes their order, and enters captions.
  • The user configures the storyboard layout and appearance.
  • JavaScript calculates the position and dimensions of every panel.
  • The preview is updated to reflect the selected settings.
  • PDF-lib and browser canvas functionality are used to generate the requested output.
  • The browser downloads the finished file.

PDF Upload Workspace

Panels and Captions

Board Settings and Preview

Final Storyboard Preview

Downloaded PDF

Project Setup

Before writing the JavaScript functionality, we need to understand how the application is organized.

The PDF Storyboard Generator combines HTML, CSS, and JavaScript. HTML provides the interface, CSS controls the appearance of the workspace and storyboard sheets, and JavaScript handles PDF processing, page previews, captions, layout calculations, and downloads.

For a standalone development project, we can organize the files like this:

pdf-storyboard-generator/
├── index.html
├── style.css
├── script.js
└── assets/

The 

index.html
file contains the application structure, including the upload area, page panels, caption fields, board settings, and preview.

The 

style.css
file controls the appearance of the application. It defines the workspace, panel grid, form controls, buttons, preview area, and responsive layout.

The 

script.js
file contains the main application logic. It loads PDF documents, renders their pages, manages captions, processes OCR requests, calculates storyboard layouts, and generates downloadable files.

The 

assets
directory can hold any additional local resources required by the project.

In the existing AllInOneTools implementation, these components are integrated into the website's tool page rather than being deployed as four separate files. The same separation of responsibilities still applies.

Libraries Used

The application uses three main JavaScript libraries or browser technologies for its PDF and image-processing workflow.

1. PDF.js

We'll use PDF.js to open PDF documents and render their pages inside the browser.

It allows JavaScript to access individual pages, retrieve their dimensions, create viewports, and draw page content onto an HTML canvas.

For this project, PDF.js is responsible for the original PDF page previews.

The application uses the PDF.js document API to retrieve pages and render them at the required dimensions. This is important because the storyboard must display a visual representation of each selected page before the user downloads the finished sheet.

2. PDF-lib

We'll use PDF-lib used when generating the final PDF document.

PDF.js and PDF-lib have different responsibilities. PDF.js reads and renders the source document, while PDF-lib creates the new storyboard PDF.

The application uses PDF-lib to create output pages, embed the original PDF pages when possible, and place the finished storyboard elements onto those pages.

Keeping the original PDF pages as vector content helps preserve text and line quality when users zoom in or print the exported document. The implementation also uses a raster-based fallback for password-protected PDFs that can't be loaded through the regular PDF embedding path.

3. Tesseract.js

This library provides optional Optical Character Recognition (OCR).

Not every PDF contains selectable text. A scanned document, for example, may contain photographs of printed pages instead of actual text data.

When the user selects the OCR option, the application loads Tesseract.js and its English language data. It then processes eligible scanned pages and attempts to extract their text for captions.

OCR is optional, so users don't need to load the OCR engine when they only want to arrange PDF pages and write captions manually.

The following example illustrates how a standalone project could include the libraries through CDN scripts:

For a production application, use library versions that you've tested and configure the matching PDF.js worker file as required by your chosen PDF.js build.

Why These Libraries Work Together

Each library has a separate responsibility.

PDF.js reads the source PDF and renders its pages. Tesseract.js optionally extracts text from scanned pages. PDF-lib creates the final storyboard PDF.

JavaScript connects these operations and manages the user interface.

This separation makes the application easier to understand and maintain. It also avoids using one library for tasks that are better handled by another.

Preparing the HTML Workspace

The interface needs several areas to support the complete storyboard workflow.

The upload area accepts the source PDF. The panel area displays rendered pages and caption fields. The board settings area contains layout and appearance controls. Finally, the preview area displays the generated storyboard sheets.

A simplified HTML structure looks like this:

This is an illustrative structure showing the main interface areas. The actual application contains additional controls, accessibility attributes, and elements for its different operations.

The 

aiot-sb
container provides a common root for the application. JavaScript can use this root to find the relevant interface elements without searching the entire website.

Selecting the Main DOM Elements

JavaScript needs references to the interface elements before it can respond to user actions.

The application starts by finding its root container and checking whether initialization has already taken place:

var root = document.getElementById("aiot-sb");
if (!root || root.getAttribute("data-aiot-sb-ready")) {
    return;
}
root.setAttribute("data-aiot-sb-ready", "1");

This prevents the application from initializing again if the script is executed more than once.

The implementation uses a small helper to find elements inside the application:

function q(selector) {
    return root.querySelector(selector);
}

For example, 

q('[data-act="browse"]')
finds the button used to open the PDF file picker.

Using a root-specific helper also helps keep the application code organized when the website contains other tools or interface components.

Defining Important Configuration Values

The application needs a few shared configuration values for its layouts and output settings.

For example, it defines supported paper dimensions and font families:

var MM = 72 / 25.4;
var PAPERS = {
    a4: [595.28, 841.89],
    letter: [612, 792],
    a3: [841.89, 1190.55],
    slide: [405, 720]
};
var PAPER_NAMES = {
    a4: "A4",
    letter: "Letter",
    a3: "A3",
    slide: "16:9 slide"
};

PDF page dimensions are commonly expressed in points, while some of the storyboard spacing settings are easier to understand in millimeters. The 

MM
conversion value helps translate between these units.

The 

PAPERS
object stores the available page dimensions. The application can use these values when calculating the size of each storyboard sheet.

The 

PAPER_NAMES
object provides readable labels for the corresponding settings.

The application also defines font families for captions and other text:

var FONTS = {
    sans: "Arial, 'Helvetica Neue', Helvetica, sans-serif",
    serif: "Georgia, 'Times New Roman', serif",
    mono: "'Courier New', Courier, monospace",
    hand: "'Segoe Print', 'Bradley Hand', cursive"
};

These values allow the storyboard renderer to use different text styles without repeating font definitions throughout the code.

Understanding the Application State

The application needs to remember information about the currently loaded PDF, its pages, captions, selected layout, and export process.

Instead of relying on individual variables scattered throughout the application, the implementation groups related information into a shared state object.

For example, the application tracks information such as:

  • The loaded PDF document.
  • The original PDF bytes.
  • The current filename.
  • Page captions.
  • Page preview data.
  • Loading and export status.

Measuring PDF Pages

Before arranging pages into storyboard panels, the application needs to know their dimensions.

PDF documents can contain pages with different sizes and orientations. Measuring each page helps the layout engine fit it correctly inside its panel.

The actual application uses the 

pageFacts()
function to measure every page and periodically update the interface while processing large PDFs.
async function pageFacts(doc, token) {
    var sizes = [];

    for (var n = 1; n <= doc.numPages; n++) {
        if (token !== state.loadToken) {
            return null;
        }

        if (n % 25 === 0) {
            setStatus(
                'Measuring pages: ' + n + ' of ' + doc.numPages + '…',
                true
            );
            await nextFrame();
        }

        var p = await doc.getPage(n);
        var vp = p.getViewport({ scale: 1 });

        sizes.push([vp.width, vp.height]);
    }

    return sizes;
}

The function starts by creating an empty 

sizes
array. It then loops through all pages using 
doc.numPages
and retrieves each page with 
doc.getPage(n)
.

The 

getViewport({ scale: 1 })
method measures the page at its original scale. The function stores the resulting width and height in the 
sizes
array.

The 

token
parameter helps prevent an outdated loading operation from continuing. If the current token no longer matches

, the function stops and returns 
null

For larger PDFs, the application updates the loading status after every 25 pages and calls

to give the browser an opportunity to update the interface.

Finally, the function returns the array containing the dimensions of all measured pages. These measurements are used later by the storyboard layout calculations.

Rendering PDF Pages on Canvas

The next task is displaying the PDF pages in the workspace.

PDF.js can render an individual page onto an HTML canvas. The canvas provides a visual representation that can be used in the page cards and storyboard preview.

The core rendering function looks like this:

async function renderPage(n, w, h) {
    var page = await state.doc.getPage(n);
    var b = page.getViewport({ scale: 1 });

    var vp = page.getViewport({
        scale: Math.min(w / b.width, h / b.height)
    });

    var c = document.createElement('canvas');
    c.width = Math.max(1, Math.round(vp.width));
    c.height = Math.max(1, Math.round(vp.height));

    var g = c.getContext('2d');
    g.fillStyle = '#FFFFFF';
    g.fillRect(0, 0, c.width, c.height);

    await page.render({
        canvas: c,
        canvasContext: g,
        viewport: vp
    }).promise;

    return c;
}

The function accepts three parameters: 

n
is the PDF page number, while 
w
and 
h
define the available width and height for the preview.

First, 

state.doc.getPage(n)
retrieves the requested PDF page. The function then creates a viewport at scale 1 to obtain the page's original dimensions.

Next, 

Math.min(w / b.width, h / b.height)
calculates a scale that fits the page inside the available space without changing its proportions.

The function creates an HTML canvas and sets its width and height using the calculated viewport dimensions. It fills the canvas with white before rendering the PDF page.

Finally, 

page.render()
draws the page onto the canvas. The function waits for rendering to finish and returns the completed canvas for use in the page previews and storyboard.

Reusing Rendered Page Previews

Rendering the same PDF page repeatedly can consume unnecessary processing time. For example, a page might be rendered once for its card preview and again when the storyboard preview is updated.

The application uses a page-picture cache to reuse previously rendered canvases.

var picCache = new Map();

// For the preview: reuse a page picture when one at least as big is already made.
async function cachedPic(n, w, h) {
    var got = picCache.get(n);

    if (got && got.w >= w * 0.92) {
        picCache.delete(n);
        picCache.set(n, got);
        return got.c;
    }

    var c = await renderPage(
        n,
        Math.ceil(w * 1.15),
        Math.ceil(h * 1.15)
    );

    picCache.set(n, { c: c, w: c.width });

    while (picCache.size > 60) {
        var old = picCache.keys().next().value;
        picCache.get(old).c.width = 1;
        picCache.delete(old);
    }

    return c;
}

The application stores rendered page previews in a JavaScript 

Map
called 
picCache
. Each entry contains the rendered canvas and its width.

When 

cachedPic()
is called, it first checks whether a cached image exists for the requested page. If the cached image is at least 92% of the requested width, the application reuses it instead of rendering the page again.

The function moves a reused entry to the end of the Map. This helps the application keep recently used previews available.

If a suitable cached image isn't available, the function calls 

renderPage()
to create a new canvas. It renders the page at 1.15 times the requested width and height, providing some extra resolution for the preview.

To control memory usage, the cache is limited to 60 entries. When that limit is exceeded, the oldest entry is removed, and its canvas width is reduced to 1 to release its drawing resources.

This caching approach avoids unnecessary PDF rendering while keeping memory usage under control, especially when users work with longer documents.

Reading Text from PDF Pages

The storyboard generator can create captions in three ways:

  • The user writes captions manually.
  • The application extracts text from the PDF.
  • OCR reads text from scanned pages.

For PDFs containing selectable text, PDF.js provides the

method.

The actual application uses the 

readTexts()
function to extract and store text from every page in the loaded PDF.
async function readTexts(token) {
    var doc = state.doc, out = [];

    for (var n = 1; n <= doc.numPages; n++) {
        if (token !== state.loadToken) {
            return;
        }

        try {
            var tc = await (await doc.getPage(n)).getTextContent();

            out.push(tc.items.map(function (it) {
                return (it.str || '') + (it.hasEOL ? '\n' : '');
            }).join(''));
        } catch (e) {
            out.push('');
        }

        if (n % 20 === 0) {
            await nextFrame();
        }
    }

    if (token !== state.loadToken) {
        return;
    }

    state.texts = out;
    refreshTags(board());
}

The function starts by accessing the loaded PDF document through 

state.doc
and creating an empty array called 
out
to store the extracted text.

It then loops through every page and calls 

getTextContent()
to retrieve its text items. The 
map()
method combines each item's text into a single string. It also adds a newline when the PDF.js item indicates the end of a line through 
hasEOL
.

If text extraction fails for a page, the function adds an empty string to the results instead of stopping the entire process.

The 

token
check prevents an older PDF-loading operation from updating the current application state. The function also calls 
nextFrame()
after every 20 pages to give the browser an opportunity to update the interface.

After processing all pages, the extracted text is stored in 

state.texts
. The application then calls 
refreshTags(board())
to update the page information displayed in the workspace.

This stored text is used later when users choose to fill empty captions automatically.

Filling Empty Captions Automatically

Once the application has extracted text from the PDF pages, it can use that text to create captions.

The important behaviour is that the application fills only empty caption fields. It doesn't overwrite captions that users have already entered.

The application uses the 

captionFromText()
helper to clean and shorten the extracted text:
function captionFromText(t) {
    var s = String(t || '')
        .replace(/\s+/g, ' ')
        .trim();

    if (letters(s) < 3) {
        return '';
    }

    if (s.length <= 200) {
        return s;
    }

    var cut = s.slice(0, 200);
    var end = Math.max(
        cut.lastIndexOf('. '),
        cut.lastIndexOf('? '),
        cut.lastIndexOf('! '),
        cut.lastIndexOf('। ')
    );

    return end > 60
        ? cut.slice(0, end + 1)
        : cut.replace(/\s+\S*$/, '') + '…';
}

Here's what this function does:

  • Converts the supplied value into a string.
  • Replaces repeated whitespace with single spaces and removes whitespace from the beginning and end.
  • Checks whether the text contains enough letters to be useful as a caption.
  • Returns the complete text if it contains no more than 200 characters.
  • For longer text, tries to end the caption at a sentence boundary. If there isn't a suitable boundary, it removes the incomplete final word and adds an ellipsis.

The application then uses 

fillFromText()
to apply the generated captions to the selected storyboard pages.
function fillFromText() {
    var bd = board(), list = bd.error ? [] : unique(bd.list), filled = 0, scans = 0;

    list.forEach(function (n) {
        if (captionFor(n)) { return; }

        var c = captionFromText(state.texts[n - 1]);

        if (c) {
            state.captions[n] = c;
            filled++;

            var ta = ui.grid.querySelector('[data-cap="' + n + '"]');
            if (ta) { ta.value = c; }
        } else if (isScan(n)) {
            scans++;
        }
    });

    if (!state.opts.captions && filled) {
        state.opts.captions = true;
        savePrefs();
    }

    redrawSoon(0);

    if (!list.length) {
        toast(bd.error || 'No pages on the board.', 'error');
        return;
    }

    toast(
        filled
            ? plural(filled, 'caption', 'captions') +
              ' filled from the page text. Edit them in the cards below.' +
              (scans
                  ? ' ' + plural(scans, 'scanned page has', 'scanned pages have') +
                    ' no text; use OCR for ' + (scans === 1 ? 'it' : 'them') + '.'
                  : '')
            : scans
                ? 'The empty pages are scans with no text. Use Read with OCR.'
                : 'Every panel already has a caption.'
    );
}

The 

fillFromText()
function starts by calling 
board()
to get the currently selected storyboard pages. It uses 
unique()
to avoid processing the same page more than once.

For each selected page, 

captionFor(n)
checks whether a caption already exists. If one is present, the function skips that page so the user's existing caption isn't overwritten.

If the caption is empty, the function retrieves the extracted text from 

state.texts
and passes it to 
captionFromText()
. When useful text is available, it saves the generated caption in 
state.captions
and updates the corresponding textarea in the page card.

If a page has no extractable text and is identified as a scan, the function increases the scanned-page counter. Users can process these pages separately using OCR.

Finally, the application enables captions if necessary, saves the updated preferences, and schedules a preview refresh. It also displays a message showing how many captions were filled or whether OCR is needed.

This allows users to generate starting captions automatically while keeping their manually written descriptions intact.

Updating the Preview

Whenever a caption or relevant setting changes, the storyboard preview needs to be refreshed.

The application uses a small scheduling function to avoid redrawing the preview immediately after every individual change:

function redrawSoon(ms) {
    clearTimeout(drawTimer);
    drawTimer = setTimeout(
        drawPreview,
        ms === undefined ? 120 : ms
    );
}

The 

redrawSoon()
function first cancels any previously scheduled preview update using 
clearTimeout()
. It then schedules 
drawPreview()
using 
setTimeout()
.

By default, the application waits 120 milliseconds before refreshing the preview. If another change happens during that time, the previous scheduled redraw is cancelled and a new one is scheduled.

This helps prevent unnecessary repeated rendering when users are typing captions or adjusting settings.

Drawing the Updated Preview

Once the redraw is scheduled, the

function calculates the current storyboard configuration and updates the visible preview canvas.

The following is the actual implementation from the application:

async function drawPreview() {
    if (!state.doc) { return; }

    var my = ++drawToken, bd = board();
    refreshTags(bd);
    syncPanel();

    if (bd.error) {
        ui.boardMsg.textContent = bd.error;
        ui.sheetPos.textContent = 'No sheets';
        ui.sheetCount.textContent = '';
        root.querySelectorAll('[data-needs-board]').forEach(function (b) {
            b.disabled = true;
        });
        return;
    }

    root.querySelectorAll('[data-needs-board]').forEach(function (b) {
        b.disabled = state.busy;
    });

    var L = bd.L, o = state.opts;
    state.sheet = clamp(state.sheet, 0, L.sheets - 1);

    ui.boardMsg.textContent = L.tight
        ? 'Captions leave little room for the pages. Use fewer caption lines, fewer rows or a smaller text size.'
        : '';

    ui.sheetPos.textContent = 'Sheet ' + (state.sheet + 1) + ' of ' + L.sheets;
    ui.sheetCount.textContent =
        plural(bd.list.length, 'panel', 'panels') + ' on ' +
        plural(L.sheets, 'sheet', 'sheets') + ', ' +
        PAPER_NAMES[o.paper] + ' ' + o.orient;

    q('[data-act="sheet-prev"]').disabled = state.sheet <= 0;
    q('[data-act="sheet-next"]').disabled = state.sheet >= L.sheets - 1;

    ui.sheetWrap.style.aspectRatio = L.W + ' / ' + L.H;

    var cssW = ui.sheetWrap.clientWidth || 600;
    var dpr = Math.min(window.devicePixelRatio || 1, 2);
    var k = cssW * dpr / L.W;

    var off = document.createElement('canvas');
    off.width = Math.round(L.W * k);
    off.height = Math.round(L.H * k);

    var done = await drawSheet(
        off.getContext('2d'),
        o,
        bd.list,
        L,
        state.sheet,
        k,
        'full',
        function (n, w, h) {
            return my === drawToken
                ? cachedPic(n, w, h)
                : Promise.resolve(null);
        }
    );

    if (!done || my !== drawToken) { return; }

    ui.sheet.width = off.width;
    ui.sheet.height = off.height;
    ui.sheet.getContext('2d').drawImage(off, 0, 0);

    off.width = 1;

    var start = state.sheet * L.per;
    var on = bd.list.slice(start, start + L.per);

    ui.sheet.setAttribute(
        'aria-label',
        'Sheet ' + (state.sheet + 1) + ' of ' + L.sheets + ': ' +
        (on.length === 1 ? 'page ' + on[0] : 'pages ' + on.join(', '))
    );

    ui.sheet.setAttribute('data-drawn', String(state.sheet + 1));
}

The function first checks whether a PDF document is loaded. It then calls 

board()
to retrieve the selected pages and calculate the storyboard layout.

The 

drawToken
value helps prevent an older preview-rendering operation from replacing a newer one. The function also calls 
refreshTags()
and 
syncPanel()
to update the page information and settings panel.

Next, it checks whether the selected board has any errors. If the selection is valid, it calculates the current sheet position and updates the sheet counter, panel count, paper information, and Previous and Next buttons.

The function then calculates the canvas scale using the available preview width and the device pixel ratio. The device pixel ratio is capped at 2 to limit the amount of rendering work.

The

function draws the selected storyboard sheet onto a temporary canvas. It receives

as a callback so previously rendered PDF page previews can be reused.

After drawing finishes, the function checks whether the operation is still current. If it is, the completed temporary canvas is copied onto the visible preview canvas.

Finally, the temporary canvas is released by reducing its width to 1. The application also updates the preview's accessibility label and records which sheet has been drawn.

This process allows users to see their storyboard changes without downloading a new PDF every time they adjust a caption or setting.

Choosing the Storyboard Layout

The tool supports three layout styles: Grid, Panels with notes, and Film strip. Each layout is designed for a different type of project.

Grid layout arranges PDF pages in rows and columns. It works well for reviewing presentation slides, comic pages, and documents.

Panels with notes provides additional writing space below each page. It's useful for lecture notes, planning, and reviewing visual material.

Film strip arranges pages as a sequence of frames. It's useful for planning videos, reels, and scenes.

The selected layout is stored in the application's state. When users choose a different layout, the application updates the number of columns and rows to provide suitable default settings.

Controlling Rows, Columns, and Paper Size

Users can choose between 1 and 6 columns and rows per sheet. This gives them control over how many PDF pages appear together.

The application also supports different paper sizes, including A4, Letter, A3, and a 16:9 slide format. Each format can be displayed in portrait or landscape orientation.

For example, a 3-column and 2-row layout can display six PDF pages on one sheet. A 4-column and 3-row layout can display twelve pages.

The application calculates the number of panels that fit on each sheet by multiplying the selected columns by the selected rows. It then determines how many sheets are needed for all selected pages.

The following function from the actual application calculates the sheet dimensions based on the selected paper size and orientation:

function sheetSize(o) {

    var b = Math.max(p[0], p[1]);

    return o.orient === 'portrait' ? [a, b] : [b, a];

PAPERS
object contains the dimensions for each supported paper format. The function retrieves the selected dimensions and arranges them according to the chosen orientation.

For portrait orientation, the shorter dimension becomes the width and the longer dimension becomes the height. For landscape orientation, these dimensions are reversed.

var per = o.cols * o.rows;
var sheets = Math.max(1, Math.ceil(list.length / per));

Here,

represents the number of panels on one sheet. The

The layout engine also calculates the available space and positions each panel so that the pages fit within the selected sheet dimensions.

Selecting PDF Pages and Their Order

Users don't always need every page in the original PDF.

The tool supports using all pages, selecting a page range, or entering a custom page sequence.

For example, a user could enter:

1-4, 9, 6

This creates a storyboard using pages 1, 2, 3, 4, 9, and 6 in that exact order.

The application uses the 

parseList()
function to process the custom page selection and check whether the requested page numbers are valid.

Here is the actual implementation from the application:

function parseList(text) {
    var t = String(text || '').trim();

    if (!t) {
        return { error: 'Type the pages, for example 1-4, 7, 5.' };
    }

    var out = [], parts = t.split(/[,;\s]+/).filter(Boolean);

    for (var i = 0; i < parts.length; i++) {
        var part = parts[i],
            m = /^(\d+)(?:\s*[-–]\s*(\d*))?$/.exec(part);

        if (!m) {
            return { error: '"' + part + '" isn\'t a page number or range.' };
        }

        var a = parseInt(m[1], 10),
            b = m[2] === undefined
                ? a
                : (m[2] === '' ? state.count : parseInt(m[2], 10));

        if (a < 1) {
            return { error: 'Pages start at 1, so "' + part + '" doesn\'t work.' };
        }

        if (b < a) {
            return { error: '"' + part + '" is backwards. Did you mean ' + b + '-' + a + '?' };
        }

        if (a > state.count) {
            return {
                error: 'Page ' + a + ' is past the end; this PDF has ' +
                    plural(state.count, 'page', 'pages') + '.'
            };
        }

        if (b > state.count) {
            return {
                error: 'Page ' + b + ' is past the end. Type ' + a +
                    '- to go to the last page.'
            };
        }

        for (var n = a; n <= b; n++) {
            out.push(n);
        }
    }

    if (out.length > 500) {
        return { error: 'That\'s ' + out.length + ' panels. Use 500 or fewer.' };
    }

    return { pages: out };
}

The function first converts the input into a trimmed string. It then splits the selection using commas, semicolons, or spaces.

The regular expression checks whether each entry is a single page number or a page range. For example, 

3
represents page 3, while 
2-5
represents pages 2 through 5.

The function also supports an open-ended range such as 

4-
. In this case, the application uses 
state.count
as the final page number.

Before adding pages to the result, it checks that page numbers start at 1, ranges are in ascending order, and no requested page exceeds the total number of pages in the PDF.

The application also limits custom selections to 500 panels. If the input is valid, the function returns an array of page numbers in the exact order entered by the user.

The 

panels()
function then uses this result when building the storyboard. If the user selects all pages instead of entering a custom list, it returns every page in the original order.

This feature is helpful when creating a storyboard from selected scenes or important slides without including the entire PDF.

Adding Panel Labels

Panel labels help users identify individual pages when reviewing or discussing a storyboard.

The application supports different label styles, including numbers, scene labels, original PDF page numbers, and no labels.

For example, a storyboard could display:

  • 1, 2, 3, 4
  • Scene 1, Scene 2, Scene 3

Drawing the Storyboard Sheet

Once the layout has been calculated, the application draws the storyboard sheet on an HTML canvas.

The drawing process places each selected PDF page inside its calculated panel area. It then adds panel labels and captions according to the user's settings.

The actual application uses the asynchronous

async function drawSheet(ctx, o, list, L, sheetIdx, k, mode, getPic) {
    var C = COLORS[o.colors] || COLORS.paper;
    var W = L.W * k;
    var H = L.H * k;
    var token = state.loadToken;
    var drawn = [];

    ctx.save();
    ctx.fillStyle = C.bg;
    ctx.fillRect(0, 0, W, H);
    ctx.textBaseline = 'alphabetic';

    var start = sheetIdx * L.per;
    var items = list.slice(start, start + L.per);

The function receives the canvas context, storyboard settings, selected page list, calculated layout, sheet index, and rendering scale.

It first selects the sheet colors and paints the background. The 

start
variable determines the first panel on the current sheet, while 
items
contains the PDF pages assigned to that sheet.

The following excerpt shows how the application fits each PDF page inside its panel and retrieves its rendered image:

for (var i = 0; i < items.length; i++) {
    var cell = L.cells[i], n = items[i], idx = start + i;
    var area = cell.img;
    var strip = o.layout === 'strip';

    if (strip) {
        ctx.fillStyle = C.bandMat;
        ctx.fillRect(
            area.x * k, area.y * k,
            area.w * k, area.h * k
        );
    } else if (o.frame) {
        ctx.fillStyle = C.mat;
        ctx.fillRect(
            area.x * k, area.y * k,
            area.w * k, area.h * k
        );
    }

    var inset = strip ? 0 :
        o.frame ? Math.min(area.w, area.h) * 0.04 : 0;

    var pr = fitPage(n, area, inset);

    var px = {
        x: Math.round(pr.x * k),
        y: Math.round(pr.y * k),
        w: Math.max(1, Math.round(pr.w * k)),
        h: Math.max(1, Math.round(pr.h * k))
    };

    drawn.push({ n: n, rect: pr });

    if (mode === 'overlay') {
        ctx.clearRect(px.x, px.y, px.w, px.h);
    } else {
        ctx.fillStyle = '#FFFFFF';
        ctx.fillRect(px.x, px.y, px.w, px.h);

        var pic = getPic ? await getPic(n, px.w, px.h) : null;

        if (token !== state.loadToken) {
            ctx.restore();
            return null;
        }

        if (pic) {
            ctx.drawImage(pic, px.x, px.y, px.w, px.h);
        }
    }
}

The

function calculates the position and dimensions needed to fit the original PDF page inside the panel without changing its proportions.

The application then uses

to retrieve the rendered page image. If the image is available,

places it on the storyboard canvas.

The function also supports an overlay mode, which leaves the page picture areas transparent. This is useful when exporting PDFs while preserving the original PDF page content.

Reading Scanned Pages with OCR

Some PDF documents contain selectable text, while others contain scanned images of printed pages.

PDF.js can extract text from pages containing actual text data. But it can't directly extract words from a scanned page that contains only an image.

To handle these pages, the application provides an optional OCR feature using Tesseract.js.

When users select Read scanned pages with OCR, the application identifies scanned pages that don't already have captions and processes them using the OCR engine.

Loading Tesseract.js When Needed

The application loads Tesseract.js only when the user requests OCR. It first checks whether the library is already available and reuses an existing loading promise if the script is still being loaded.

Here's the actual 

loadTesseract()
implementation:
var tessPromise = null;

function loadTesseract() {
    if (window.Tesseract) {
        return Promise.resolve(window.Tesseract);
    }

    if (tessPromise) {
        return tessPromise;
    }

    tessPromise = new Promise(function (resolve, reject) {
        var s = document.createElement('script');
        s.src = TESS + 'tesseract.min.js';
        s.async = true;

        s.onload = function () {
            if (window.Tesseract) {
                resolve(window.Tesseract);
            } else {
                tessPromise = null;
                reject(new Error('engine'));
            }
        };

        s.onerror = function () {
            tessPromise = null;
            reject(new Error('engine'));
        };

        document.head.appendChild(s);

        setTimeout(function () {
            reject(new Error('engine'));
        }, 45000);
    });

    return tessPromise;
}

The function checks 

window.Tesseract
to see whether the OCR library is already available. If it is, the function returns it immediately.

If the library is still loading, the existing 

tessPromise
is returned instead of creating another script request.

Otherwise, the application creates a script element, sets its source to the Tesseract.js library, and adds it to the document. The 

onload
and 
onerror
handlers detect whether loading succeeds or fails.

Creating the OCR Worker

After the library loads, the application creates a Tesseract worker configured for English text recognition.

The following excerpt comes from the actual

checkCancel();

    corePath: TESS_CORE,

await w.setParameters({ debug_file: '/dev/null' });

The 

createWorker()
method initializes the OCR engine with the English language data. The worker and core paths tell Tesseract.js where to load its supporting files.

The logger reports language-loading and text-recognition progress. The application uses this information to update its progress indicator while OCR is running.

Generating the Final Storyboard PDF

Once the user is satisfied with the layout and captions, the application can generate the final PDF.

This process uses PDF-lib to create a new PDF document. The application creates one output page for each storyboard sheet. It then places the original PDF pages inside their calculated panel positions and adds the storyboard's titles, labels, and captions.

Creating the PDF Document

async function exportPdf(snap, token) {
    await engine();

    var PL = window.PDFLib,
        L = snap.L,
        o = snap.o,
        list = snap.list;

    var out = await PL.PDFDocument.create(),
        src = null,
        embedded = {};

            src = await PL.PDFDocument.load(

            );

            src = null;
        }

        var c = document.createElement('canvas');

        c.width = Math.round(L.W * k);
        c.height = Math.round(L.H * k);

        var drawn = await drawSheet(
            c.getContext('2d'),
            o,
            list,
            L,
            s,
            k,
            'overlay',

            x: at.x,
            y: at.y,
            width: ew,
            height: eh,
            rotate: PL.degrees(-rot)

in 
full
mode. This draws the PDF page previews together with the storyboard titles, labels, captions, and other selected settings.

The 

pngBytes()
helper converts the completed canvas into PNG data. Each image is added to the 
files
array with a filename containing its sheet number.

After processing all sheets, the application checks how many PNG files were generated. A single sheet is downloaded directly as a PNG. Multiple sheets are packaged into a ZIP archive using 

makeZip()
.

This format is useful for sharing storyboard previews in presentations, messages, and other applications.

Downloading Individual Page Pictures

The third export option is Page pictures (ZIP).

Unlike the PNG sheets option, this export contains individual pictures of the PDF pages selected for the storyboard.

The application renders each selected page separately and places the resulting PNG files into a ZIP archive.

Exporting Individual PDF Pages

The actual application handles this option inside the 

exportJob()
function. It first creates a unique list of selected pages and then renders each page individually.

Here's the actual implementation:

var pages = unique(list),
    out = [];

for (var i = 0; i < pages.length; i++) {
    checkCancel();

    setProgress(
        i / pages.length,
        'Saving page ' + pages[i] +
        ' (' + (i + 1) + ' of ' + pages.length + ')…'
    );

    var pg = await state.doc.getPage(pages[i]),
        vb = pg.getViewport({ scale: 1 }),
        sc = Math.min(
            2,
            Math.sqrt(12e6 / (vb.width * vb.height))
        );

    var pc = await renderPage(
        pages[i],
        vb.width * sc,
        vb.height * sc
    );

    out.push({
        name: 'panel-' +
            pad2(list.indexOf(pages[i]) + 1) +
            '-page-' + pad2(pages[i]) + '.png',
        data: await pngBytes(pc)
    });

    pc.width = 1;
}

save(makeZip(out), state.base + '-panels.zip');

toast(
    'Saved ' +
    plural(out.length, 'page picture', 'page pictures') +
    ' in a ZIP.'
);

The function first calls 

unique()
to remove duplicate page numbers from the selected list.

It then processes each page individually. The 

getPage()
method retrieves the original PDF page, and 
getViewport()
obtains its dimensions.

The scale calculation limits the rendering scale to 2 while keeping the rendered page within approximately 12 million pixels. This helps control memory usage when processing large pages.

The 

renderPage()
function creates the page image, while 
pngBytes()
converts the canvas into PNG data.

Each image is added to the 

out
array with a filename containing both its panel position and original PDF page number. This makes it easier to identify the pictures and maintain their storyboard order.

Finally, 

makeZip()
packages all the generated PNG images into a ZIP archive, which the browser downloads.

This option is useful when users want to work with individual PDF page pictures rather than complete storyboard sheets.

Performance and Important Considerations

Rendering large PDFs and generating high-resolution images can consume significant browser memory.

The application uses page-preview caching, temporary canvases, progress reporting, and cancellation controls to manage this work.

For better results, use fewer panels per sheet when working with large documents. A3 paper can also provide more room when a storyboard contains many panels.

Remember that layout preferences are remembered on the device, but the PDF and captions remain in the current browser tab. Download your work before closing the tab.

Demo: PDF Storyboard Generator

You can try the finished application here:

PDF Storyboard Generator – AllInOneTools

Upload a PDF, arrange its pages, add captions, customize the storyboard, and download the finished result.

Conclusion

Building a PDF Storyboard Generator combines several useful browser technologies into one application.

PDF.js handles PDF loading and page rendering. Tesseract.js provides optional text recognition for scanned pages. PDF-lib creates the final storyboard PDF, while HTML canvas handles previews and image exports.

By connecting these components with JavaScript, we can create a practical tool for organizing presentation slides, comic pages, scripts, and other PDF documents.

The project also demonstrates how browser-based applications can process documents locally without requiring users to upload their files to a server.

With the complete workflow in place, users can turn ordinary PDF pages into organized storyboard sheets that are easier to review, print, and share.

entries.content:
A top-down action roguelite only works when combat feels sharp, rooms feel connected, and every run asks you to trade power for risk. Godot 4 has the tools for that, but most tutorials stop before those systems fit together into a game someone else can open and play.

We just published a comprehensive 10-hour course on the freeCodeCamp.org YouTube channel that will teach you how to build a complete top-down action roguelite in Godot 4.7.2, from an empty project to an exported game. This course is taught by Omar Zaki, creator of Coding Quests, and most lessons include a Your Turn section where you build the next piece yourself before you see the solution.

Here is what the course covers:

  • Dash Combat & I-Frames

    Build weighty movement, aiming, and a dodge with invincibility frames so combat feels fair instead of cheap.
  • Enemies, Telegraphs & a Boss Tell

    Create five enemy types from a shared base, then add a boss with a clear warning before the hard hit lands.
  • Procedural Connected Rooms

    Generate random floors of linked rooms in code, track where you are, and lock a fight until the room is clear.
  • Items, Corruption & Shops

    Stack items into builds, take corruption that trades power for fragility, and risk gold at shops and a gambling altar.
  • Run Loop, Unlocks & Export

    Wire death, permanent unlocks, a title screen, sound, and an export so a stranger can download and play your game.

Watch the full course on the freeCodeCamp.org YouTube channel (10-hour watch).
