entries.content:
If you've built a couple of React Native apps, the following probably feels familiar. You start with a 

colors.ts
file and a simple 
Button
component. Everything looks fine at first. Then the design changes a few times, and that small color file starts growing. Your Button also picks up another prop every time someone asks for a slightly different style.

The setup works at first, but after a few design changes, even a small update can mean checking several files across the project.

Here's what a typical color file looks like after a while:

export const colors = {
  primary: '#6e4836',
  primaryPressed: '#5a3a2b',
  textPrimary: '#261d16',
  textSecondary: '#72665e',
  // and forty more
};

And here's what a typical 

Button
looks like after a few redesigns:

These are simplified examples, but you get the idea. The color object keeps growing, and the Button collects more props to handle every new design request.

Each change seems reasonable when you make it. But the annoying part comes later, when changing one design decision means checking several files to see that nothing else has changed unexpectedly.

Part of the problem is how many component libraries are distributed. Their code lives in 

node_modules
, so you usually customize them through the props and options they expose. When the library doesn't cover your exact use case, you add another prop or override. Keep doing that and the component can become harder to maintain than the original problem you were trying to solve.

This is one reason I like shadcn/ui's approach. You don't install a traditional component package and treat its components as fixed. The CLI copies the source code into your project, where you can change it whenever you need to. For React Native, there's a project built around the same idea called React Native Reusables.

To make this practical, I'll use React Native Reusables, Expo, and Uniwind to build a cart and checkout screen for a coffee shop's pickup orders. It includes order items with quantity controls, a pickup-time dropdown, a name field, an "own cup" toggle, a bill summary, a checkout bar that stays at the bottom, and an order-confirmation dialog. If you want to see how reusable sections come together in complete interfaces, you can also browse shadcn templates.

I'll also point out a few things that are easy to miss when working with these components, including:

  • How shadcn/ui and its CLI work, and why you own the component code
  • How design tokens (named colors) replace a 
    colors.ts
    file
  • How to use components such as Card, Select, Switch, and AlertDialog in React Native
  • How to handle mobile-specific issues, such as safe areas, keyboards, and tap targets
  • How to switch between light and dark mode, and how to change the whole theme from one file

Table of Contents

Prerequisites

To follow along, you should have:

  • Node.js 20 or newer. You can use pnpm, npm, yarn, or bun. The commands in this tutorial use pnpm, so swap the prefix if you use something else.
  • Basic knowledge of React and TypeScript, especially hooks such as 
    useState
    .
  • Some familiarity with React Native, such as 
    View
    , 
    Text
    , and 
    ScrollView
    . You don't need to know Tailwind, but it helps.
  • Optional: Xcode or Android Studio if you want to run the app in a simulator. Everything also runs in a web browser through React Native Web, and that's how the screenshots in this tutorial were taken.

You don't need any accounts or API keys, and nothing here costs money.

Tools You Will Use

Before creating the app, let's look at the tools in this project. Each one has a specific job, and knowing that will make the setup easier to follow.

shadcn/ui is a collection of UI components for the web. It's not installed as a package. Instead, a command-line tool (CLI) copies the source code of each component into your project, and from then on the code is yours to edit.

React Native Reusables is the React Native version of shadcn/ui. It gives you components such as Button, Card, Select, and Dialog that are written for React Native and styled with Tailwind-style class names. It uses the same CLI idea as shadcn/ui.

RN Primitives is a React Native port of Radix UI, which is the library that shadcn/ui uses for behavior on the web. A "primitive" is a component that handles the behavior but has no styling. For example, the 

select
primitive knows how a dropdown opens and closes and how it's announced to screen readers, but it has no colors or borders. React Native Reusables adds the looks on top.

Uniwind is a tool that lets you style React Native components with Tailwind CSS class names, such as 

className="bg-primary p-4"
. It converts those classes into regular React Native styles while the app is being bundled, so there's no extra work at runtime. Nativewind does a similar job, and React Native Reusables supports both. This tutorial uses Uniwind.

Expo and Expo Router provide the project setup, the development server, and file-based navigation. If you have used Next.js, Expo Router works in a similar way.

How shadcn/ui Works

The React Native Reusables documentation opens with a quote from shadcn:

This is not a component library. It is how you build your component library.

You won't add shadcn/ui as a regular dependency in 

package.json
. It uses a registry instead. A registry is a collection of JSON files hosted on a server. Each file describes a component and includes the information the CLI needs to add it to your project. When you run the CLI, it reads the relevant file and copies the component's source code into your project.

To see what this looks like, here's the registry entry for the Badge component. A Badge is a small label, such as the "Medium" tag next to a coffee in the cart you will build later. This is a shortened version of the real file:

{
  "$schema": "https://ui.shadcn.com/schema/registry-item.json",
  "name": "badge",
  "type": "registry:ui",
  "title": "Badge",
  "author": "@mrzachnugent",
  "description": "Displays a badge or a component that looks like a badge.",
  "dependencies": ["@rn-primitives/slot"],
  "registryDependencies": ["https://reactnativereusables.com/r/uniwind/text.json"],
  "files": [
    {
      "path": "./node_modules/@rnr/registry/src/uniwind/components/ui/badge.tsx",
      "content": "import { TextClassContext } from '@/components/ui/text';\nimport ...",
      "type": "registry:ui"
    }
  ]
}

The file is public, so you can look at it yourself:

curl https://reactnativereusables.com/r/uniwind/badge.json

Here's what the important fields mean:

  • content
    holds the full source code of the component, stored as a string.
  • dependencies
    lists npm packages that the component needs. The CLI installs these first.
  • registryDependencies
    lists other registry entries that the component needs. In this case, Badge needs the Text component, which is a small wrapper around React Native's 
    Text
    that you will read about in Step 3. When you run the CLI to add Badge, it also adds Text for you because of this field.

That's how a component gets from the registry into your app. The registry stores the component information, and the CLI uses it to create the files in your repository. React Native Reusables uses the shadcn CLI behind the scenes, so you can follow the same workflow when adding React Native components.

There are a few reasons this approach is useful when you're building an app:

  • You own the file: A component such as 
    components/ui/button.tsx
    sits in your repository and shows up in your Git diffs. If you want a darker pressed state, you edit that line. You don't need to invent a new prop, maintain a fork, or open an issue.
  • Design lives in named colors instead of props: Colors are declared once as named roles, such as 
    primary
    , 
    muted
    , 
    border
    , and 
    destructive
    . You then use them in class names, like 
    className="bg-primary"
    . This replaces the 
    colors.ts
    file from the introduction, because there's one place that defines your colors, and every component reads from it. You'll set this up in Step 2.
  • Behavior comes from a separate package: Things such as focus handling, open and close state, and screen reader support live in RN Primitives. You only write the styling.

There's one trade-off to keep in mind. Since the component code is copied into your project, updates from the registry aren't applied automatically. If a bug is fixed upstream, you'll need to run the CLI again with 

--overwrite
. If you have customized that component, you may also need to reapply your changes. This is worth considering before you make large changes to several components.

What React Native Reusables Gives You

At the time of writing, React Native Reusables includes thirty components: accordion, alert, alert-dialog, aspect-ratio, avatar, badge, button, card, checkbox, collapsible, context-menu, dialog, dropdown-menu, hover-card, input, label, menubar, popover, progress, radio-group, select, separator, skeleton, switch, tabs, text, textarea, toggle, toggle-group, and tooltip. The available components cover many of the building blocks you need for a typical app interface.

React Native is different from the web in several ways, so the components can't be an exact copy of the web version. The documentation lists the main differences, and you'll run into each of them in this tutorial. If you're also building web interfaces with shadcn/ui, shadcn components can be useful when you need more ready-made examples to work from.

The differenceWhat it meansWhere you will see it
Portals need a 
PortalHost
 On the web, floating content such as dropdowns renders into 
document.body
. React Native has no 
document.body
, so you need a 
PortalHost
component to render into.		 Step 7
Styles don't cascadeA text color set on a parent view doesn't reach the text inside it, so React Native Reusables uses a 
Text
component with a workaround.		 Step 3
There are no 
data-*
attributes		 Web shadcn changes styles based on attributes like 
data-state
. React Native has none, so variants depend on props and state.		 Step 7
Icons take props instead of classesIcon libraries expect 
color
and 
size
props, so icons are wrapped to accept class names.		 Step 3

What You're Building

We'll build a cart and checkout screen for a coffee shop where customers place an order and pick it up at the counter. The screen uses twelve components from the registry. While putting it together, I'll also explain a few React Native details that are easy to miss, including how dropdowns are rendered, how safe areas affect the layout, and how to keep the checkout bar visible while the rest of the page scrolls:

Part of the screenComponents usedThe mobile problem it teaches
Item rowsCard, Avatar, Badge, ButtonNo cascading styles, no 
truncate
, small tap targets
Quantity stepperButton, IconIcons take props, not classes
Pickup timeSelect, LabelDropdowns need a portal
Name fieldInput, LabelThe keyboard can cover the field
Own cup toggleSwitch, LabelMaking the label text tappable
BillSeparator, TextDigits that don't line up
Checkout barButton, AlertDialogNo 
position: fixed
, and the home indicator

Here's the finished screen:

The complete code is available in the GitHub repository if you want to compare your work with the final result.

Step 1: Create the App

We can let the React Native Reusables CLI create the initial project for us. It sets up Expo Router, the styling configuration, the theme file, and a few starter components. Run the following command to get started:

pnpm dlx @react-native-reusables/cli@latest init

Answer the CLI's Questions

The CLI asks four questions.

What is the name of your project? The name you type becomes the folder name. It suggests 

my-app
.

Select a template. There are three options, and the one you need isn't the one selected by default:

❯ Minimal (Nativewind)
  Minimal (Uniwind)
  Clerk auth (Nativewind)

Press the down arrow once and choose Minimal (Uniwind). This is the one choice that's tricky to change later. Nativewind and Uniwind are two different ways to use Tailwind in React Native, and the CLI keeps a separate registry for each one. The components it writes for Uniwind are different from the ones it writes for Nativewind, so the code in this tutorial won't match if you pick Nativewind.

Would you like to install dependencies? Choose yes, and select the package manager you use.

Would you like to initialize a Git repository? Choose yes. You're about to replace the starter screen, and having a commit to compare against is helpful.

Look at the Project Structure

The CLI creates the following files:

shadcn-react-native-app/
├── app/
│   ├── _layout.tsx        # ThemeProvider, Stack, and the PortalHost
│   ├── +html.tsx          # web only, the root HTML shell
│   ├── +not-found.tsx
│   └── index.tsx          # the starter screen
├── components/ui/
│   ├── button.tsx
│   ├── icon.tsx
│   └── text.tsx
├── lib/
│   ├── theme.ts           # the same palette again, in JavaScript
│   └── utils.ts           # cn()
├── global.css             # the theme tokens
├── components.json        # the shadcn config, same as on the web
├── metro.config.js        # withUniwindConfig
└── uniwind-types.d.ts     # generated, do not edit

Before moving on, let's take a look at a few files in this structure. You'll use them throughout the tutorial:

  • components.json
    is the same shadcn configuration file used on the web. It tells the CLI where to put components (
    @/components/ui
    ) and where the 
    cn()
    helper lives (
    @/lib/utils
    ).
  • global.css
    holds your theme tokens, which you'll learn about in Step 2.
  • lib/utils.ts
    exports 
    cn()
    , a helper that combines class names and resolves conflicts between them.
  • app/_layout.tsx
    contains a 
    PortalHost
    component. It looks like leftover scaffolding, but you must not delete it. Step 7 explains why.

Uniwind reads 

global.css
while Metro bundles the app and turns your class strings into React Native style objects. This happens at build time, so a long 
className
string doesn't slow down your app.

Run the App

Start the development server:

pnpm dev

Press 

w
to open it in the browser, 
i
for the iOS simulator, or 
a
for Android. The starter screen has a theme toggle in the header, which shows that the theme setup is working.

You can also run a diagnostic command at any point if something seems wrong:

pnpm dlx @react-native-reusables/cli@latest doctor

It checks your setup and reports which styling library it detects. For this project, the output should be:

ℹ Styling Library: Uniwind
✔ All checks passed.

If it says Nativewind, fix that before you add any components.

Once the setup is working, you should see the starter screen. Try the theme toggle in the header to make sure light and dark mode both work, and check that the console is free of errors:

Step 2: Understand the Theme File

Now that the app is running, let's look at its theme setup. The 

global.css
file is where we'll define the colors used by the components. If you've previously kept these values in a 
colors.ts
or 
theme.ts
file, this is the setup that replaces it.
@import "tailwindcss";
@import "uniwind";

@import "tw-animate-css";

@theme {
  --radius: 10px;
  --radius-sm: calc(var(--radius) - 4px);
  --radius-md: calc(var(--radius) - 2px);
  --radius-lg: var(--radius);
  --radius-xl: calc(var(--radius) + 4px);

  --spacing-hairline: hairlineWidth();
}

@layer theme {
  :root {
    @variant light {
      --color-background: oklch(1 0 0);
      --color-foreground: oklch(0.145 0 0);
      --color-card: oklch(1 0 0);
      --color-primary: oklch(0.205 0 0);
      --color-muted-foreground: oklch(0.556 0 0);
      --color-border: oklch(0.922 0 0);
      /* the rest of the list */
    }

    @variant dark {
      --color-background: oklch(0.145 0 0);
      --color-foreground: oklch(0.985 0 0);
      --color-card: oklch(0.205 0 0);
      --color-primary: oklch(0.922 0 0);
      --color-muted-foreground: oklch(0.708 0 0);
      --color-border: oklch(1 0 0 / 10%);
      /* the rest of the list */
    }
  }
}

There are two conventions in this file that you need to know.

First, the 

--color-
prefix creates the class names. When you declare 
--color-primary
, Tailwind automatically creates 
bg-primary
, 
text-primary
, and 
border-primary
. If you declare 
--primary
instead, you only get a CSS variable that nothing uses.

This is important because most shadcn theme generators produce the web format, where the variables are named 

--primary
. If you paste that output without renaming the variables, nothing breaks, but nothing changes either. Step 12 shows you how to convert them.

Second, 

@variant light
and 
@variant dark
replace 
:root
and 
.dark
. On the web, dark mode works by adding a 
.dark
class to the page. A phone has no page to add a class to, so Uniwind manages the switch. When you call 
Uniwind.setTheme
, it swaps the active values. You'll use this in Step 11.

You may also notice that the file uses 

oklch()
colors. Phones don't have a browser to read that format, but Uniwind converts the colors to a format React Native understands while bundling, so you can use modern color syntax anyway.

The Palette Also Exists in 
lib/theme.ts

If you open 

lib/theme.ts
, you'll find the same colors again as a JavaScript object. This duplication is needed because React Navigation, which draws the header and screen background, reads colors from a plain JavaScript object and can't read CSS variables. As a result, you have to keep two copies of your palette in sync. Step 12 shows what happens when they differ.

Try It: Change One Color

Let's change one of the tokens to see how the theme works. Update the primary color in the light theme to a value that's easy to notice:

--color-primary: oklch(0.6 0.24 25);

Save the file and look at the starter screen. The Browse the Docs button is now red, even though you didn't edit 

button.tsx
:

Notice that every component using 

bg-primary
picks up the new color. You only changed one token, but the button updated without touching its component file. Change the value back before continuing.

Step 3: Read Three Core Components

The starter project already gives us three components: 

Text
, 
Button
, and 
Icon
. I'd take a few minutes to look through them before building the screen. They introduce patterns you'll see again in the other registry components.

The Text Component

In React Native, styles don't cascade the way they do in CSS. If you set a text color on a 

View
, the text inside it doesn't inherit that color. This is a problem for a component such as
, which needs its label to be white. The label is a 
Text
component that the Button doesn't control, because it comes in through 
children
. On the web, the Button would simply set a color and let it flow down to the label.

React Native Reusables solves this with React context. This is the code in 

components/ui/text.tsx
:
const TextClassContext = React.createContext(undefined);

function Text({ className, asChild = false, variant = 'default', ...props }) {
  const textClass = React.useContext(TextClassContext);
  const Component = asChild ? Slot : RNText;
  return (
    
  );
}

A parent component, such as Button, puts a class string into the context. Every 

Text
inside it reads that string and applies it. Your own 
className
still wins because it comes last in the 
cn()
call.

The 

Text
component also has a 
variant
prop with options like 
h1
to 
h4
, 
p
, 
code
, 
lead
, 
large
, 
small
, and 
muted
. For example,
gives you the mobile version of 
text-muted-foreground text-sm
. The variants also set the 
role
and 
aria-level
props, so screen readers announce headings correctly without any extra work.

The Button Component

The Button in 

components/ui/button.tsx
uses 
cva
(class-variance-authority) the same way the web version does. Here's a shortened version:
const buttonVariants = cva(
  cn(
    'group shrink-0 flex-row items-center justify-center gap-2 rounded-md shadow-none',
    Platform.select({
      web: "focus-visible:border-ring focus-visible:ring-ring/50 ... transition-all",
    })
  ),
  {
    variants: {
      variant: {
        default: cn(
          'bg-primary active:bg-primary/90 shadow-sm shadow-black/5',
          Platform.select({ web: 'hover:bg-primary/90' })
        ),
        /* ... */
      },
    },
  }
);

There are four differences from the web version:

  • flex-row
    is written out: React Native lays out children in a column by default, which is the opposite of CSS. Every horizontal layout in this tutorial includes 
    flex-row
    for that reason.
  • active:
    replaces 
    hover:
    : A finger can't really hover, so 
    active:
    is the pressed state on a phone.
  • Web-only classes are wrapped in 
    Platform.select
    : Classes such as 
    focus-visible:ring-[3px]
    mean nothing in React Native, so they're only included in the web build.
  • A 
    TextClassContext.Provider
    wraps the 
    Pressable
    : This uses the context from the previous section, and it's why
    has white text automatically.

The Icon Component

Icons from 

lucide-react-native
take 
color
and 
size
as props, not as class names. The 
Icon
component in 
components/ui/icon.tsx
teaches Uniwind how to convert one into the other:
const StyledIcon = withUniwind(IconImpl, {
  size: { fromClassName: 'className', styleProperty: 'width' },
  color: { fromClassName: 'className', styleProperty: 'color' },
});

This code reads the 

width
from the class string and passes it as 
size
, and it reads the 
color
and passes it as 
color
. That's why
works the way you would expect. 
withUniwind
is useful any time you use a third-party component that takes props where you want to use classes.

You don't need to run anything for this step. The important part is understanding what 

TextClassContext
is doing. Once that clicks, the other components in the registry are much easier to follow.

Step 4: Add the Components You Need

We already have three components from the template. For the checkout screen, we need a few more. The CLI can add all of them in one go:

pnpm dlx @react-native-reusables/cli@latest add card separator input label select switch badge alert-dialog avatar

The CLI detects that you're using Uniwind and writes the matching versions. It also installs any required 

@rn-primitives
packages and adds a file called 
native-only-animated-view.tsx
, which Select and AlertDialog use for their animations.

The output looks like this:

ℹ Styling Library: Uniwind
✔ Created 10 files:
  - components/ui/separator.tsx
  - components/ui/input.tsx
  - components/ui/label.tsx
  - components/ui/switch.tsx
  - components/ui/avatar.tsx
  - components/ui/native-only-animated-view.tsx
  - components/ui/card.tsx

Problem 1: Portals and the PortalHost

When a dropdown opens, it needs to appear above the other content on the screen. For that reason, 

SelectContent
isn't rendered in the same place where you declare it in the component tree. It uses 
@rn-primitives/portal
to render the content in another part of the app. This technique is called a portal.

On the web, a portal renders into 

document.body
, and every page has one. React Native has nothing like that. So the portal package keeps a list of portal contents in memory, and a component called 
PortalHost
reads that list and displays it. This is a simplified version of that code from 
node_modules/@rn-primitives/portal/dist/index.js
:
var DEFAULT_PORTAL_HOST = "INTERNAL_PRIMITIVE_DEFAULT_HOST_NAME";
var updatePortal = (hostName, name, children) => { /* writes into the map */ };
function PortalHost({ name = DEFAULT_PORTAL_HOST }) { /* reads the map */ }

If no 

PortalHost
is mounted, the content is saved but never displayed. The dropdown opens into nothing, and you get no error or warning.

Problem 2: Safe Area Insets

There's another issue to consider when showing a dropdown on a phone. Parts of the screen are reserved for the operating system, such as the area around the notch and the home indicator. If a dropdown opens near the bottom of the screen, one of its options could appear underneath the home indicator. In that area, a tap may be handled by the operating system instead of your app.

To avoid this, pass the safe area insets to the content:

const insets = useSafeAreaInsets();
const contentInsets = { top: insets.top, bottom: insets.bottom, left: 16, right: 16 };

The 

insets

in

One more thing to watch out for is the value returned by 

onValueChange

So the label is correct on native, but on the web it's a copy of the value. If you only test in a simulator, you won't notice this problem.

Platform.select
, but it stays inside the class string.

Three things aren't handled by 

setTheme
, and if you forget them, you end up with a screen that's only partly dark. The template already sets up the first two.

1. The Navigation Header

React Navigation takes its colors from a plain object, so the root layout needs to pass it the right one:

const { theme } = useUniwind();

2. The Status Bar

The clock and battery icons are drawn by the operating system, so you need to tell it which style to use. Without this, you can get dark text on a dark bar.

3. Saving the Choice

Uniwind.setTheme
only applies to the current session. The next time the app starts, it follows the system setting again. To keep the user's choice, save it with 
expo-secure-store
or 
AsyncStorage
and call 
setTheme
when the app starts. You can call 
setTheme('system')
to go back to following the operating system.

When you tap the header icon, the cards, borders, inputs, switch, header, and status bar should all change together. You can explore more ready-made shadcn blocks if you want examples of how these components are used in larger interfaces:

Look for anything that stays light while the rest goes dark. A light header usually means the 

ThemeProvider
is not receiving the new 
NAV_THEME
.

Step 12: Create Your Own Theme

The screen is currently using the default gray theme. Let's change it to a coffee-inspired palette with warm cream backgrounds and brown accents. This will also help us see why the palette needs to be updated in both 

global.css
and 
lib/theme.ts
.

Update the Tokens

Replace the 

@layer theme
block in 
global.css
with this coffee palette:
@layer theme {
  :root {
    @variant light {
      --color-background: oklch(0.98 0.008 75);
      --color-foreground: oklch(0.24 0.02 60);
      --color-card: oklch(1 0.003 90);
      --color-card-foreground: oklch(0.24 0.02 60);
      --color-popover: oklch(1 0.003 90);
      --color-popover-foreground: oklch(0.24 0.02 60);
      --color-primary: oklch(0.44 0.06 45);
      --color-primary-foreground: oklch(0.99 0.01 85);
      --color-secondary: oklch(0.93 0.03 80);
      --color-secondary-foreground: oklch(0.35 0.05 45);
      --color-muted: oklch(0.95 0.012 80);
      --color-muted-foreground: oklch(0.52 0.02 60);
      --color-accent: oklch(0.92 0.04 78);
      --color-accent-foreground: oklch(0.32 0.05 45);
      --color-destructive: oklch(0.577 0.245 27.325);
      --color-border: oklch(0.89 0.02 75);
      --color-input: oklch(0.89 0.02 75);
      --color-ring: oklch(0.44 0.06 45);
    }

    @variant dark {
      --color-background: oklch(0.17 0.012 60);
      --color-foreground: oklch(0.96 0.008 85);
      --color-card: oklch(0.22 0.016 62);
      --color-card-foreground: oklch(0.96 0.008 85);
      --color-popover: oklch(0.22 0.016 62);
      --color-popover-foreground: oklch(0.96 0.008 85);
      --color-primary: oklch(0.85 0.09 75);
      --color-primary-foreground: oklch(0.22 0.03 55);
      --color-secondary: oklch(0.29 0.022 62);
      --color-secondary-foreground: oklch(0.94 0.01 85);
      --color-muted: oklch(0.27 0.018 62);
      --color-muted-foreground: oklch(0.72 0.015 75);
      --color-accent: oklch(0.31 0.03 65);
      --color-accent-foreground: oklch(0.95 0.01 85);
      --color-destructive: oklch(0.704 0.191 22.216);
      --color-border: oklch(1 0 0 / 12%);
      --color-input: oklch(1 0 0 / 15%);

If you don't want to choose thirty colors by hand, you can generate a theme with the shadcn theme generator or tweakcn. Both export CSS variables, but you need to make two changes before the output works in this project:

  • Rename each variable to include the 
    --color-
    prefix. For example, 
    --primary
    becomes 
    --color-primary
    .
  • Move the 
    :root
    block inside 
    @variant light
    , and the 
    .dark
    block inside 
    @variant dark
    .

Also remove 

--radius
from what you paste, because the template already defines it along with the derived sizes. Remove any 
--shadow-*
variables too, since nothing in the registry reads them.

Update lib/theme.ts

After you save and reload, the result looks like this:

The page is cream, the button is brown, and the badges have the right color, but the header is still white with a visible line under it. The reason is that React Navigation draws the header using 

lib/theme.ts
, and that file still has the old palette. Nothing is broken and nothing warns you, so this mistake is easy to miss. If you're designing the same interface in Figma, the shadcn Figma resources can also help you keep the design and implementation aligned.

Update 

lib/theme.ts
to match:
import { DarkTheme, DefaultTheme, type Theme } from 'expo-router/react-navigation';

export const THEME = {
  light: {
    background: '#fcf8f3',
    foreground: '#261d16',
    card: '#fffffd',
    primary: '#6e4836',
    border: '#e3d9cd',
    destructive: '#e7000b',
    /* the rest of the list */
  },
  dark: {
    background: '#130e0a',
    foreground: '#f4f1ec',
    card: '#201913',
    primary: '#f1c68b',
    border: '#3a3129',
    destructive: '#ff6467',
    /* the rest of the list */
  },
};

export const NAV_THEME: Record<'light' | 'dark', Theme> = {
  light: {
    ...DefaultTheme,
    colors: {
      background: THEME.light.background,
      border: THEME.light.border,
      card: THEME.light.background,
      notification: THEME.light.destructive,
      primary: THEME.light.primary,
      text: THEME.light.foreground,
    },
  },
  dark: {
    ...DarkTheme,
    colors: {
      background: THEME.dark.background,
      border: THEME.dark.border,
      card: THEME.dark.background,
      notification: THEME.dark.destructive,
      primary: THEME.dark.primary,
      text: THEME.dark.foreground,
    },
  },
};

This isn't a direct copy of 

global.css
, so three points need explanation:
  • Use hex colors instead of 
    oklch()
    : Uniwind converts 
    oklch()
    for your classes, but React Navigation does not, so give it a format that React Native can read directly. You can convert a color with any online converter, or paste the 
    oklch()
    value into your browser's developer tools color picker and read the hex value.
  • Map React Navigation's 
    card
    to your 
    background
    , not your 
    card
    . The two names look the same but mean different things. In shadcn, 
    card
    is a raised surface on top of the page. In React Navigation, 
    card
    is the background of the screen and header. If you map them by name, the header ends up a shade lighter than the page. You won't notice this with the stock template because it uses the same value for 
    card
    and 
    background
    . It only shows up once you create a theme where cards stand out from the page, like this one.
  • Use a solid color in place of a transparent border. In dark mode, 
    --color-border
    is 
    oklch(1 0 0 / 12%)
    , which is white at 12% opacity. A navigation theme needs a solid color, so work out what that border looks like on your background and use that value.

After this change, the header and page match in both light and dark mode, and you didn't edit any component files:

Switch between light and dark a few times and watch the header. If it's a shade lighter or darker than the page, one of the values in 

lib/theme.ts
is still from the old palette.

Common Mistakes and How to Fix Them

If you're coming from web development, some of these differences may catch you off guard. I've collected the issues covered in the tutorial in the table below, along with the fix for each one. You can refer back to it when something doesn't behave as expected.

Conclusion

In this tutorial, we built a coffee shop cart and checkout screen with React Native Reusables, Expo, and Uniwind. We added the order rows, pickup options, bill summary, fixed checkout bar, and confirmation dialog. We also looked at how the registry and CLI add component source code to the project and how the theme tokens control the app's colors.

One thing worth getting into the habit of is checking the component source when something doesn't behave the way you expect. Since the components live in your project, you can open them and see how they work. That's how we understood the difference in the Select label between web and native. It also makes customization easier because you can see which part of the component needs to change instead of adding more workarounds around it.

You can find the complete project in the GitHub repository. If you run into an issue or want to compare your code with the finished screen, clone the repository and check the implementation. If you're looking for more complete starting points for your next project, take a look at shadcn templates.

I captured the screenshots using the React Native Web build at a phone-sized viewport. The same project also runs on iOS and Android. I've called out the platform differences in the relevant sections, including the Select label and portal host in Step 7, safe area handling in Step 9, and haptics in Step 10.

entries.title: What a CAPTCHA Farm Attack Actually Looks Like

entries.content:
CAPTCHAs are something most of us have come across while browsing the internet. Sometimes we're asked to identify traffic lights in pictures, solve a small puzzle, or simply tick a box to confirm we're human. Websites use these challenges to help distinguish real users from automated bots.

But there's an interesting problem with this approach. What happens when a bot doesn't need to solve the CAPTCHA itself because a real person can solve it for them?

This is how CAPTCHA farms work. Attackers use services where real people solve CAPTCHA challenges on behalf of automated programs. The person completing the challenge is human, but the activity happening behind it may still be controlled by a bot. This makes it harder for websites to identify suspicious requests, even when their CAPTCHA system appears to be working correctly.

Here, we'll look at how CAPTCHA farm attacks work, why attackers use human solvers, and what makes these attacks difficult to detect. We'll also go through some of the security measures developers can use to identify suspicious activity and better protect their websites.

What We'll Cover:

What Is a CAPTCHA Farm Attack?

To understand how these attacks work, it helps to distinguish between the two primary ways attackers deal with verification gates: machine-driven recognition and human-driven outsourcing.

In an automated CAPTCHA-solving attack, an attacker uses computer vision models, optical character recognition (OCR), or neural networks to parse the challenge image and guess the answer without human intervention.

This approach is fast and computationally cheap, but it frequently fails when security vendors update their visual distortions, introduce interactive logic puzzles, or assess human-like mouse kinematics.

A CAPTCHA farm attack takes the opposite route. Instead of attempting to outsmart the defensive algorithm with software, the attacker routes the challenge to a human solving service. These commercial operations maintain large networks of manual workers who solve puzzles continuously around the clock. By inserting a human into the loop, the attacker converts what should be a technical roadblock into an outsourced labor pipeline.

The attack doesn't break the cryptography or reverse-engineer the underlying challenge code. Instead, it relies on a CAPTCHA relay attack: software manages the speed and scale of the attack, while real human eyes provide the cognitive validation the website expects.

Behind the Scenes: The Four-Part Infrastructure

A functional CAPTCHA farm is neither an ad-hoc group of rogue hackers nor an obscure black-box script. It's a commercial, multi-tiered infrastructure built around standard web development protocols.

Four distinct components work together to make the relay happen in a matter of seconds.

First is the attacker’s automated script. This client bot typically runs headlessly via browser automation tools like Puppeteer, Playwright, or custom HTTP client libraries. The script navigates to a target platform, such as a user registration portal, and fills in usernames, passwords, and demographic fields at machine speed until it hits a defensive challenge.

Second is the CAPTCHA-solving platform's API. Commercial solver platforms act as brokers between abuse operators and manual laborers. When the attacker's script encounters a challenge, it intercepts the site's public key, the challenge URL, and the visual assets, packaging them into an HTTP POST request directed at the solving service’s application programming interface (API).

Third is the distributed human workforce. Workers access these services through dedicated web dashboards, mobile apps, or browser plug-ins. When the API receives a task from an attacker, it pushes the image directly onto a worker’s screen. The worker identifies the bicycles or fire hydrants, types the distorted characters, or drags the puzzle slider into place, earning a microscopic payout, often ranging from $0.50 to $2.00 per thousand puzzles solved.

Fourth is the payload delivery back to the target. Once the worker submits the correct solution, the broker API returns the generated verification token back to the attacker’s script. The script injects this validation token into the target website's hidden form field and fires the final submission request. To the receiving server, the request bears an authentic verification signature generated by a real human session.

How an Attack Unfolds: A Step-by-Step Look

To see how these parts interact in practice, consider a credential-stuffing or mass-account registration campaign against an online service.

  • Initiation: The attacker's script dispatches an HTTP request to establish a session with the target registration page, populating the input fields with generated credentials.
  • Challenge trigger: The target application evaluates the incoming request. Detecting an unfamiliar IP address or an incomplete browser fingerprint, it triggers a CAPTCHA modal, pausing the registration sequence until a valid solution token is supplied.
  • Extraction and dispatch: The bot reads the page DOM, captures the puzzle iframe parameters, site key, and challenge payload, and forwards this data to the CAPTCHA farm API.
  • Human execution: The farm's queuing system allocates the challenge to an active human worker. The worker completes the puzzle within an average response window of 10 to 25 seconds.
  • Token retrieval: The worker’s response yields an official validation token from the CAPTCHA provider's origin server. The solving farm's API returns this signed string to the attacker’s script.
  • Form finalization: The script injects the token into the page's response payload (such as g-recaptcha-response) and submits the form. The website’s backend queries the CAPTCHA provider's verification API, receives a confirmation that the challenge was successfully passed, and creates the account.

The entire loop completes well before typical session timeouts kick in, leaving the target server with no obvious visual anomaly to flag.

Why Attackers Rely on Human Solvers

Building and maintaining custom neural networks to break modern visual challenges requires constant development effort. Defensive providers frequently alter noise patterns, camera angles, distortion algorithms and semantic puzzles specifically to break automated image classifiers.

Human solvers bypass this arms race entirely because the human visual cortex processes semantic context effortlessly. A person instantly understands what constitutes a "motorcycle," even if the image is cropped awkwardly, partially obscured by street foliage, or rendered under strange lighting.

This human adaptability is supported by extensive security research. In a foundational study, Towards Understanding the Security of Modern Image Captchas and Underground Captcha-Solving Services, researchers analyzed the commercial ecosystem across 152 solving platforms. They found that human-solving services achieved near-flawless accuracy rates across complex, diverse image challenges where purely automated computer vision solvers repeatedly struggled or degraded over time.

Outsourcing the problem is also remarkably inexpensive. Because labor pools are drawn from regions with low living costs, attackers can bypass thousands of protective checkpoints for less than the price of a cup of coffee. The workflow is highly scalable: software handles millions of connections, while human labor is summoned on-demand only for the few seconds required to clear a barrier.

What CAPTCHA Farms Target

CAPTCHA farms rarely serve as self-contained attacks. Instead, they act as an operational enabler for wider abusive campaigns across the web.

First, they enable mass fake account creation. Malicious actors generate millions of disposable profiles on social media, dating networks, and developer platforms to distribute phishing links, spam search engines, or run coordinated disinformation campaigns.

They also facilitate credential stuffing. When attackers test databases of leaked usernames and passwords against banking or retail portals, defensive systems usually throw a CAPTCHA after a handful of failed attempts. Solver APIs allow the credential-testing bots to continue cycling through login credentials uninterrupted.

Inventory hoarding and scalping is another common use case. High-demand retail drops, concert tickets, and travel bookings are frequent targets. Security researchers tracking real-world bot traffic at DataDome documented an operation where an attacker combined bot automation with a CAPTCHA farm to orchestrate 18 million automated ticket-scalping attempts, successfully bypassing front-line interactive verification.

And they enable data scraping at scale. Web crawlers harvesting competitive pricing, directory databases, or intellectual property frequently utilize solver APIs whenever protected search and discovery pages present challenge gates.

In every case, the CAPTCHA farm doesn't execute the underlying abuse: it merely removes the specific verification tripwire meant to halt it.

Why These Attacks Are Difficult to Stop

Stopping CAPTCHA farms is inherently difficult because they exploit the core assumption behind standard challenge-response security: that the entity answering the challenge is the entity making the request.

This systemic blind spot is analyzed in the research paper On the Security and Usability of Dynamic Cognitive Game CAPTCHAs, which evaluated how puzzle formats hold up against relay systems. The study demonstrated that regardless of how cognitively engaging, gamified, or technically dynamic a test is, relay architectures successfully decouple cognitive processing from the requesting client. The server receives a mathematically legitimate, human-generated solution token, making the puzzle itself effectively irrelevant.

Also, attackers route their client requests through residential proxy networks. The initial HTTP request comes from one residential IP address, the CAPTCHA is rendered by an automated browser mimicking common hardware profiles, and the solution is completed remotely. The defender’s server can't verify the physical proximity between the solver and the requesting client, creating an asymmetric advantage for the attacker.

How Websites Can Defend Themselves

Because human solvers can easily clear visual and cognitive challenges, treating a solved puzzle as a blanket guarantee of trustworthiness is no longer a viable defensive strategy. Web applications require a defense-in-depth model that monitors behaviors before, during, and long after a verification challenge appears.

Behavioral Telemetry and Biometrics

Automated scripts can easily spoof screen resolutions and user-agent strings, but reproducing organic human cursor movement across an entire page requires far more work. Real users demonstrate micro-deviations, variable acceleration curves, pauses, and continuous mouse tremors.

When a CAPTCHA farm attack takes place, there's often a distinct behavioral mismatch: the form fields are filled out instantaneously or via scripted keyboard events, followed by an abrupt pause while the remote worker solves the puzzle, followed by an instantaneous token injection. Monitoring telemetry across the whole lifecycle of the page exposes this artificial stitching.

Network and Device Fingerprinting

Defenders must assess context beyond the single page interaction. Inspecting TCP/IP packet behavior, TLS fingerprints (JA3/JA4 fingerprints), HTTP/2 frame parameters, and device APIs reveals whether the underlying runtime environment is a standard consumer browser or an orchestrated automation tool running inside a data center.

Modern Rate-Limiting Models

Relying entirely on puzzle solving often introduces accessibility barriers for real users while doing little to stop funded attackers. As explored in research published by the Association for Computing Machinery regarding mCaptcha and Proof-of-Work Rate Limiting, defensive architectures can enforce cryptographic proof of work puzzles at the transport layer.

By forcing the connecting client's CPU to compute complex mathematical problems proportional to the platform's current traffic load, defense systems raise the economic and computational cost of running automated campaigns, neutralizing attacks without demanding manual human puzzle-solving.

Post-Authentication Anomaly Detection

Passing an authentication challenge should never grant unconditional trust. Web architectures should monitor post-login activity for anomalous actions:

  • Does an account immediately attempt hundreds of data queries per minute right after registering?
  • Does it immediately navigate directly to high-value purchase endpoints without loading associated asset stylesheets or images?
  • Does the session change IP ranges and geographic locations between the initial page load and the final transaction?

Identifying these signals allows security teams to invalidate sessions even if the initial challenge was solved cleanly.

Security Beyond the Checkbox

CAPTCHA farms show why websites can't rely on a single security check to keep automated attacks away. Even when someone successfully completes a CAPTCHA, the request may still be part of an automated operation.

CAPTCHAs are designed to check whether a person can solve a particular challenge. But they can't tell whether that person is the actual user trying to access the website or someone solving the challenge on behalf of a bot. This is one of the reasons CAPTCHA farms can bypass a security measure that would normally stop automated traffic.

For developers, this means a completed CAPTCHA should be treated as just one part of the verification process. Websites also need to monitor user behavior, network activity, and suspicious requests to identify possible attacks. Combining these checks makes it easier to spot activity that a CAPTCHA alone might miss.

Conclusion

CAPTCHA farms make it difficult for websites to tell whether a completed verification challenge actually came from a legitimate user. Even when a real person solves the puzzle, the request may still be part of an automated attack.

For developers, this means it's worth paying attention to what happens before and after a CAPTCHA is completed. Things like unusual login attempts, repeated requests, unexpected changes in user behavior, and suspicious account activity can provide useful clues.

Using CAPTCHA alongside rate limiting, behavioral monitoring, and other security checks can help websites identify these attacks more effectively. It's also important to review these protections regularly as attackers change how they operate.

entries.title: Introducing Socrates and the New freeCodeCamp Forum
entries.summary: freeCodeCamp just turned 12 years old. And so did our beloved forum. And today I'm thrilled to say that the forum is now focused on discussions rather than Q&A. This is thanks to Socrates, a new tool
entries.content:
freeCodeCamp just turned 12 years old. And so did our beloved forum. And today I'm thrilled to say that the forum is now focused on discussions rather than Q&A.

This is thanks to Socrates, a new tool we just launched. Socrates is built right into the freeCodeCamp curriculum. It can look at your code and give you hints to help you get unstuck.

When you ask Socrates for help, first it references the thousands of hints and test cases we've human-authored for the curriculum. And if none of those cover your situation, Socrates will come up with new hints to guide you.

Here're some photos of Socrates in action:

Socrates is live now. Try it on the freeCodeCamp curriculum.

Socrates frees up the forum to serve as a place for discussions

Since most people will be getting unstuck using Socrates, we think far fewer people will need to ask for help on the forum. So we can instead use the forum as a place to talk with fellow human beings about our hobbies, passions, studies, and goals.

Over the years we've built up a super chill mod team. Folks from all over the world with a broad range of backgrounds. These knights and dames keep the vibe positive and productive, and keep out the bots and spammers.

So here's what I want you to do.

  • Read our 85-word-long code of conduct.
  • Sign into the freeCodeCamp forum, read some threads, reply to some threads, and start some threads of your own.

As you use the forum, we'll trust you with more and more power there. More people will come to recognize you as a chill person who brings useful insights.

If you're looking for an alternative to divisive social media, a place where people talk WITH each other rather than PAST each other, well this is it. You've hit the jackpot.

I'm spending a lot of time there and hope you'll do the same.

Shout out to all the mods for helping everybody get the most out of the limited minutes in their day. See you on the forum.
